headline: Federated Hermes views Space's lock-up expiry as a market stress test that was handled well, signalling long-term investor interest
reasoning: Sherman discusses Space's first lock-up expiry, involving approximately 911 million shares worth around $101 billion — potentially the largest single-company share release in history. He notes the market digested it well, aided by a solid earnings number the day before. The only negative reaction came from higher-than-expected CapEx spending. He views the smooth digestion as a positive sign for the market and highlights the stock's unique positioning at the intersection of the AI trade and the space economy, which supports long-term demand.
quote: They had I believe it was 911 million shares that were eligible to trade. It was the first of nine stages. They've broken up the explorations over time. On the order of 101 billion in value as far as the shares that were eligible to trade. So it could have been a, you know, a real large chunk for the market to have to digest, likely the largest amount of shares for a single company in history, if not the most. Certainly right up there. And the market handled it swimmingly. We got through a good earnings number the day before with fewer losses and expected better revenues. The one little hiccup where the market did react, I guess this was on Thursday, I want to say was in there CapEx spending, which no surprise. You know, it was bigger than the market anticipated. So I think the stock reacted poorly to that. But it digested, you know, the the expiration quite swimmingly. It's been up the last two days. So I think it's a good sign for the market overall. And you know, it's a company that an awful lot of people almost need to participate. And they sit, you know, kind of right at the junction there of the AI trade in the space economy. So it makes sense that there's a long term a lot of long term interest.
episode_title: “Phenomenal” US earnings highlight these stock standouts

headline: Federated Hermes bullish on US equities as earnings season delivers blow-out results with over 50% year-on-year index growth

He sees no reason why the rally cannot continue and describes the firm's overall posture as 'pretty optimistic'.

It's really astounding how diversified it's been. We're seeing double digit growth of about eight of the 11 sectors. Ten of the 11 are positive overall. headline: Middle East conflict and Fed leadership uncertainty create near-term volatility risk but are unlikely to derail global growth, per Federated Hermes scenario analysis

He points to oil forward curves remaining well-behaved as evidence the market has correctly priced a resolution, even as spot prices bounced. He acknowledges the conflict is feeding through to inflation and is compounded by uncertainty around new Fed leadership and upcoming US midterm elections, which together could produce near-term volatility but should not reverse the case for being overweight equities.
quote: What we've learned to do, I think, is do a kind of scenario analysis where you have at least likely and most likely and kind of maybe your most optimistic scenario and our kind of middle of the road, most likely one was that there were too many players involved to allow this to, you know, go in absolutely the wrong direction, where the entire economy was disrupted globally... You never saw oil futures, you know, going forward, you know, call for the summer contract, really get out of hand. So while the short end spot prices have been bouncing a bit, the curve has been pretty well behaved, uh, gave us confidence that our idea that this would ultimately get resolved in some form or another without disrupting everything... headline: Federated Hermes overweight equities at ~6% above benchmark in multi-asset funds, favouring diversification across growth, value, small caps and EM
reasoning: John Sherman says Federated Hermes is telling investors in its multi-asset funds to be approximately 60% overweight equity, or roughly 6% above the maximum overweight. After years of frustration with a narrow Mag Seven-led market, the team has diversified the overweight across large growth, large value, small caps and international markets, with a tilt toward emerging markets. Sherman notes the market has broadened out, which is positive for stock pickers who can exploit volatility beneath the surface headline index gains. He would consider adding further on any reasonable near-term volatility.
quote: We remain pretty optimistic overall. So we are telling our investors, you know, in our multi-asset funds to be almost 60%. Call it overweight equity. So if you know if your max amount is ten to be overweight, we're overweight 6%. We'd like to be very diversified in that overweight. We come off a couple of years where like a lot of folks that are really focused on stock picking, we're kind of frustrated with the very narrow market led by the Mag seven. And thankfully that has broadened out. So we have diversified our overweight across both large growth, large value, small caps internationally. We tend to favor em a little bit. We just think it makes sense to kind of spread it around. And again, it's a good market for stock pickers where you get a lot of volatility beneath the surface.

headline: Federated Hermes watching AI spending circularity carefully but not yet seeing signs of a bubble
reasoning: Sherman flags that some earnings numbers need to be discounted for non-recurring items, particularly Google and Amazon marking up investments in other companies by roughly $150 billion in the quarter. He identifies the core risk as a timing mismatch: hyperscalers are spending heavily now, downstream companies benefit immediately, but whether the hyperscalers themselves ultimately benefit proportionally remains an open question that will take years to answer. He notes the firm is in the optimistic camp on AI broadly but is watching carefully for bubble signals.
quote: The circularity is absolutely a potential problem. What you really have is a timing difference between, you know, the hyperscalers spending now the downstream companies benefiting from that immediately. And the question is going to be down the road. Do the hyperscalers end up benefiting proportionally at least income wise, to what they're spending? And of course, more broadly, does it play out, as we all hope, for the economy as a whole? And, you know, we're in that camp at the moment, but it's a very positive thing. We're watching very carefully for kind of signs of a bubble, and we just don't think we see it yet.
